svg.title: Agreeing to pay: a hosted service, or the room
svg.desc: A hosted transaction service exposes the proposal, the signer set, who has signed and the timing before anything reaches a chain. Inside the encrypted room none of that leaves — but the threshold is enforced by the room and never by the zone.
svg.text: Agreeing to pay, two ways
The strongest comparison in the build — and the one that has to carry its counterweight in the same frame.
THE USUAL SHAPE — A HOSTED SERVICE
The proposal and the signatures pool in a service.
Everyone involved fetches from it and posts back to it.
The operator sees what was proposed, the full signer set,
who has signed and who has not, and the timing — and
frequently, so does anyone who has the URL.
All of it before anything reaches a chain.
WHAT AN OUTSIDER LEARNS
The negotiation leaks before the
transaction does.
HERE — INSIDE THE ENCRYPTED ROOM
An approval is an ordinary message.
It inherits the conversation's authentication exactly as
text does — it carries its author, and the fold that builds
the card deduplicates by author.
So nobody in the room can forge an approval, replay
someone else's, or approve twice. The count is a real
count of real members — and no service is in the loop.
WHAT AN OUTSIDER LEARNS
That a conversation is active, and when.
Not what was proposed, not who agreed,
not how many.
AND THE PART THAT TRAVELS WITH IT, ALWAYS, IN THE SAME FRAME
The zone does not enforce the threshold.
The account that pays is single-key. Whoever proposed the payment could have paid it without waiting for anyone, and the only
record that they waited is the conversation. "2 of 3" is enforced by the room, never by the chain — an outside observer sees an
ordinary transfer with no policy attached to it.
An approval is not bound to what it approves.
Approvals name a proposal by an id this app minted. Nothing commits to an environment, an account, a serialization slot or an
expiry, so their scope is this conversation by convention rather than by construction.
What would close the first, and where it actually stands.
An account whose policy the zone itself enforces. lez-multisig implements exactly this flow — but against a local sequencer,
with no documented deployment to this testnet, and its proposal state and calls are public accounts. Status: partial.
So today the choice is a chain-enforced threshold or a shielded amount — not both. That is a live trade, not a missing feature.
